report:
Contrary to your initial expectation, the evidence demonstrates that **denosumab (Prolia) does reduce the risk of vertebral fractures** in patients with osteoporosis.

### Key Evidence

* **Primary Trial Data:** The pivotal 3-year FREEDOM trial evaluated postmenopausal women with osteoporosis receiving biannual denosumab injections versus a placebo. Denosumab significantly reduced the risk of new radiographic vertebral fractures, with a cumulative incidence of 2.3% in the denosumab group compared to 7.2% in the placebo group (https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/nejmoa0809493).
* **Mechanism of Action:** Denosumab is a monoclonal antibody that targets and inhibits RANKL (receptor activator of nuclear factor-κB ligand). By blocking RANKL from binding to osteoclasts, denosumab decreases osteoclast-mediated bone resorption, increases bone density, and reinforces skeletal strength (https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/cell-and-developmental-biology/articles/10.3389/fcell.2020.00325/full).
* **Broader Efficacy:** Systematic reviews and clinical trial analyses consistently confirm that denosumab reduces the overall incidence of new vertebral, nonvertebral, and hip fractures (https://www.aafp.org/afp/2019/0501/od1, https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3617467/).

### Conclusion

The answer to your question is **yes**. High-quality randomized controlled trials confirm that denosumab significantly lowers the risk of vertebral fractures in postmenopausal osteoporosis.

### Sources
* New England Journal of Medicine (FREEDOM Trial): https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/nejmoa0809493
* Frontiers in Cell and Developmental Biology: https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/cell-and-developmental-biology/articles/10.3389/fcell.2020.00325/full
* American Academy of Family Physicians (AAFP): https://www.aafp.org/afp/2019/0501/od1
* PubMed Central (NCBI): https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3617467/
